name: PT Bank BTPN Syariah Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank BTPN Syariah - a low price for a high-return ultra-micro franchise
frontmatter.summary: BTPS trades below book while earning a low-teens return on equity. The market is pricing the 2023-24 credit shock as permanent; the field-force model has restored profitability and the first nine months of 2026 profit already covers most of last year's total. We initiate at BUY with a target of Rp1,622.
thesis: The franchise earns a sustainable ROE near 12.8% against a cost of equity of 11.9%, yet trades well below book value - the gap is the mispricing, not a caution.
The credit cycle has turned; management reports NPF improving while FY2025 profit reached IDR1,200.0bn and the first nine months of 2026 profit IDR1,010.0bn [S2][S5].
Capital is not the constraint - CAR of 59.0% at September 2026 - so growth is self-funded and the payout can stay at 55.0% [S2][S6].
The dividend is Rp92 per share against a Rp1,020 price, and the board has applied for a buyback of up to IDR1,000.0bn [S6][S9].
{'What we disagree with': 'the price implies a sustainable ROE below the cost of equity, which this book has only earned in the credit-shock trough.'}

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results and proposed final dividend
Annual general meeting - final dividend approval and buyback execution
nine-month 2027 results - first clean read on the post-buyback capital position

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Bank BTPN Syariah at **BUY** with a target of Rp1,622, a total return of 68.1% from the Rp1,020 close including the Rp92 next-twelve-month dividend [S0]. The stock trades below a book value that is still compounding while the bank earns a forecast return on equity of 13.0% [S0][S5]. Our target is the weighted output of a warranted price-to-book calculation, a residual-income model and a dividend discount model, each built on the same ROE path. The methods span a range rather than a point: the dividend discount model sits below the blend because it capitalises only distributed earnings, and we reconcile that in the valuation section rather than calling the spread a narrow band.

The variant view is about the durability of the return, not the level of the share price. The market is treating the 2023-24 ultra-micro credit cycle as the normal state of this book. Management's numbers say otherwise: net profit rose to IDR1,200.0bn in FY2025 and reached IDR1,010.0bn in the first nine months of 2026 on total operating income of IDR4,735.8bn [S0][S2][S5], while the capital ratio sits at 59.0% [S2]. The result is a bank that is simultaneously over-capitalised and under-earning on its equity, which is exactly the combination that supports a re-rating as the payout puts the excess capital to work, with the buyback as unquantified upside if it is approved [S9].

Three things move the value. First, the through-cycle cost of risk: the market is capitalising the trough rather than the cycle, and every point of loss on the book is worth a disproportionate share of sustainable ROE. Second, financing growth: the book grew at a double-digit year-on-year rate to IDR11,000.0bn at September 2026 against an industry pool of IDR757,320.0bn, which requires the field force to keep adding customers at the same productivity [S2][S10]. Third, the payout: the board declared a Rp85.70 per-share FY2025 dividend at the April 2026 meeting and applied for a buyback of up to IDR1,000.0bn at the October 2026 extraordinary meeting, so the excess-capital discount narrows as capital is returned [S6][S9].

Bank BTPN Syariah is the only Indonesian commercial bank whose entire business is the ultra-micro segment, served through female community officers who run weekly group meetings. The model is expensive to operate and cheap to fund, which is why its margin is high and its credit losses are lumpy. Readers familiar with the bank should treat the exhibits as the argument; the prose is the interpretation.

BTPS is a sharia commercial bank focused on the ultra-micro segment, a subsidiary of PT Bank SMBC Indonesia (formerly BTPN), which consolidates it into a Japanese-SMBC-controlled group [S0]. The bank takes deposits from affluent retail customers and institutions, and channels the funding almost entirely into group-based sharia financing to productive low-income women, organised in *sentra* (customer centres) served by Community Officers who visit weekly [S5]. The operating model is the moat and the cost base at once: the same field force that underwrites the financing collects it, and its physical presence is why the bank's loss rates, high in absolute terms, are not the loss rates of a remote-lending book.

The product set has broadened. Beyond group financing, the bank runs individual financing for customers whose businesses have outgrown the group product, financing to non-bank financial institutions with a measured risk profile, and a funding franchise that distributes retail sukuk and cash-waqf linked deposits [S2][S11][S13]. The stated strategic intent is diversification of growth sources without abandoning the ultra-micro core [S13]. Deposits are gathered through branch and digital channels; total assets at September 2026 were IDR24,000.0bn [S2].

The group structure matters for governance and for the buyback. SMBC Indonesia holds the controlling stake, the free float is 30.3%, and the foreign-controlled parent imposes a capital and compliance discipline that shows up in a CAR of 59.0% [S0][S2]. We cannot verify the provisioning stance - no source we hold discloses a provision line or an NPF ratio - so we treat the book as unmeasured rather than as conservatively provisioned, and the base case assumes no release. The board is led by a president director with a finance and operations director alongside; the senior team has been stable through the credit cycle [S0].

The competitive position is unusual. The bank is not a challenger to the large Islamic windows of the systemic banks in corporate or mortgage finance; it is the leader - effectively the creator - of the ultra-micro group-lending category, with a customer-acquisition model that cannot be replicated quickly because it depends on trained field staff and on the social capital of the *sentra* [S5]. The addressable market is the unbanked and under-banked mass market, which is why the industry's sharia financing book of IDR757,320.0bn is still small relative to the conventional system [S10].

The ultra-micro segment in Indonesia has historically been served by subsidised government programmes, pawnshops and informal lenders. A commercial bank entering it at scale has to build the field infrastructure before it earns a rupiah; that is why the franchise has few direct competitors of comparable size.

Indonesian sharia banking held 7.5% of national banking assets at September 2026 on an asset base of IDR1,108,450.0bn [S10]. Financing outstanding reached IDR757,320.0bn and grew at a double-digit annual rate, in line with the faster-growing end of the system, while deposits grew more slowly - the industry financing-to-deposit ratio rose to 88.2% [S10]. Faster asset growth against slower funding growth is the structural backdrop for every sharia bank in the country, and it explains why deposit competition, not loan demand, is the binding constraint on growth.

Asset quality at the industry level is benign: gross NPF was 2.3% in September 2026, improving slightly month on month [S10]. BTPS's own NPF is not disclosed in the releases we obtained, but management states repeatedly that it is falling, and the profit trajectory is consistent with that - the first nine months of 2026 profit of IDR1,010.0bn against a FY2025 total of IDR1,200.0bn [S2][S5]. The gap between the industry's low NPF and BTPS's much higher through-cycle credit cost is the most important analytical point in this report: the industry number describes a book dominated by corporate and consumer finance, not ultra-micro group lending, and using it to calibrate BTPS's cost of risk would understate the true charge by an order of magnitude.

Regulation is supportive at the margin. OJK continues to tighten prudential standards for sharia banks - it issued a new capital-adequacy rule for sharia people's credit banks in 2026 - while the sharia market share creeps up [S10]. For a bank with a CAR of 59.0%, capital rules are not a constraint; for smaller competitors they are [S2]. The BI rate path at 5.8% sets the cost of the deposit franchise [S10].

Five forces, briefly. Rivalry is low at the ultra-micro group-lending end and high in deposit gathering; entrants are numerous but sub-scale, and the industry's 7.5% asset share tells you how little the sharia system has taken from the conventional banks [S10]. Buyer power is diffuse - millions of small borrowers - but the bank's dependence on repeat customers creates a soft form of lock-in. Supplier power sits with depositors, whose switching costs are low, which is why the funding franchise is the weaker leg. Substitutes are informal moneylenders and the government's subsidised credit programmes. The threat of new entrants is real in digital lending but not in the field-force model that BTPS actually runs.

The structural driver we care about is not the industry growth rate but the spread between financing yield and deposit cost. Sharia banks cannot use the policy rate as a direct lever because profit-sharing deposits reprice with the asset side; the practical effect is that a bank with a high-yielding ultra-micro book enjoys a wider spread than a conventional lender when rates fall and a narrower one when deposit competition is acute. That asymmetry is why BTPS's margin, not its volume, is the variable to watch through the cycle, and why we model income almost flat in FY2026E even as the financing book grows [S0][S2].

Sharia banking in Indonesia has grown faster than conventional banking for most of the past decade from a small base. The constraint has never been demand; it has been the supply of trained human capital and the cost of educating customers about sharia products.

Total operating income peaked at IDR5,043.6bn in FY2022, fell to IDR4,906.0bn as the credit cycle forced the bank to reprice and de-risk, and was IDR4,735.8bn in FY2025 [S0]. Net profit followed the same arc but more violently: IDR1,779.5bn, then IDR1,080.5bn, then IDR1,061.3bn, before recovering to IDR1,200.0bn [S0]. A revenue line that falls by a tenth while profit falls by two-fifths, then profit recovering ahead of revenue, is the signature of a provisioning cycle, not of a franchise losing its economics. The bank did not lose customers; it absorbed losses and then repriced.

The FY2026 build is anchored to the observed nine months, not to a provision release. Total income is modelled at IDR4,783.2bn, essentially flat before the larger financing base feeds through, because the first nine months of 2026 show the bigger book has not yet produced a bigger income statement [S0][S2]. Profit is modelled at IDR1,294.7bn, which is the reported nine-month profit of IDR1,010.0bn plus a fourth quarter deliberately set below the nine-month quarterly average, the same shape as Q4-2025, which also ran under its own run-rate [S5][S2]. We do not credit a normalising cost of risk in the base case. That distinction matters: the gap between income and profit in the forecast comes from the fourth-quarter assumption and the observed run-rate, and we cannot decompose it further because no source we hold discloses provisions.

The cost of risk is the input we cannot source, and we say so rather than invent it. Neither the quarterly releases [S2][S3][S8] nor the data pack [S0] carries a provision line, an NPF ratio or a cost-of-risk figure for BTPS; the only qualitative statement is management's that NPF is falling and punctual repayment is improving [S11]. We therefore hold the through-cycle charge at the FY2025 level for the whole forecast instead of assuming it normalises, and the bear case is explicitly the 2023-24 loss rate returning. Two consequences follow. First, the FY2026E ROE of 13.0% is not a recovery call; it is the 2025 economics applied to a slightly larger book. Second, the sensitivity of the target to the cost of risk is the single most important number in this report, and it is exactly the number our disclosure set does not let us pin. The statutory accounts for the first three quarters would settle it; we will rebuild the model from them the moment they are available.

No cost-of-risk decomposition is published for a second reason: the house bank build needs net interest income, non-interest income, opex and provisions separately, and this issuer's data pack carries only a combined total operating income with no deposit, provision or NIM line [S0]. Building NIM times leverage minus credit cost minus cost-to-income would mean inventing four inputs and calling the product a model. We instead drive ROE directly, calibrate it to the reported ratio (the engine's calibration gate tests FY2025A reported 12.9% against the model path and flags any drift), and argue the mechanism in this section. That is a deliberate, disclosed deviation from the method card, and the reader should hold it against us: the moment the split is available, the four-line build replaces this.

Capital and returns. Equity was IDR9,959.0bn at FY2025 and the model carries it to IDR10,593.5bn after deducting IDR660.2bn of cash dividends, which is the Rp85.70 per share FY2025 dividend approved at the April 2026 annual meeting and paid during 2026 [S6][S0]. The Rp92.43 per share we model as declared for FY2026E is the following year's dividend and is deducted in the following year's roll, not this one - the roll's cash-dividend line therefore runs a year behind the declared DPS by construction. Book value per share rises from Rp1,293 to Rp1,375, and ROE from 12.9% to 13.0% [S0]. A capital ratio of 59.0% on a IDR24,000.0bn balance sheet means retained earnings are not needed to fund growth at any plausible rate; they are excess, and the board is treating them as such [S2][S9].

Funding and liquidity. Deposits are not separately disclosed in our sources, which is a genuine gap: the pack carries no deposit line and the releases give assets only [S0][S2]. The balance sheet we can observe is total assets of IDR24,000.0bn at 30 September 2026, and equity of IDR9,959.0bn at FY2025 [S2][S0]; we do not attempt an earning-asset build, and the model's ROE path is driven off equity, not off an assumed balance-sheet base. The industry context is that sharia deposits grew more slowly than financing through 2026, with an industry FDR of 88.2% [S10]; a bank that is over-capitalised and liquid is the least exposed to that squeeze, which is why we do not treat the funding gap as a risk to the base case but do carry it as the bear case's transmission channel.

Earnings quality. The bank is a lender, so the accruals screen is replaced by the provisioning screen. Provisions are not disclosed in our sources either; what we can say is that the FY2025 recovery is accompanied by management statements that NPF is falling and repayment punctuality is improving [S11][S13]. That is management assertion, not audited evidence, and it is the weakest link in this initiation. The buyback and the dividend are cash events, which is a harder signal of real earnings than any statement about asset quality [S6][S9].

One caveat on the history: the pack reports total operating income without the split between financing margin and fee income, and the releases we obtained do not break it out either [S0][S2]. We therefore model the whole income line at the net margin and carry non-interest income at nil, which understates fee income from sukuk distribution and individual financing but keeps the profit path honest. When the FY2026 accounts are published, the split should be rebuilt from the notes and the model re-based; until then, the reader should treat the income line as an aggregate rather than as a margin times a balance sheet.

Cost and provisioning are the two lines that decide whether the ROE path holds. The field force is the cost base: community officers are salaried and trained in-house, so the cost line behaves like a fixed cost in the short run and falls as a share of income only when the book grows. That is why we let cost-to-income ease rather than cut it, and why a stall in financing growth would hurt margins twice - through lower income and through a cost ratio that does not flex. On provisioning, the base case holds the FY2025 charge flat rather than assuming it normalises, because the 2023-24 cycle showed this book can absorb several years of elevated losses and no source we hold lets us measure where in that cycle the current charge sits [S0][S2]. The base case therefore embeds no provision release at all; the entire gap between our target and the current price comes from the ROE the book already earns, the capital return, and the price sitting below book - not from a credit recovery we cannot evidence.

Banks are valued on equity, not on enterprise value, and the house method card mandates a residual-income framework with a warranted price-to-book cross-check. We apply exactly that: the primary weight sits on warranted P/BV built from a sustainable ROE, a cost of equity and a growth rate, with residual income and dividend discount as the cross-checks.

The cost of equity is built, not assumed: 7.4% long-dated IDR sovereign yield less the 1.6% sovereign default spread gives the rupiah risk-free rate, plus a beta of 0.90 times the sum of the 4.2% mature-market equity risk premium and the 2.5% Indonesia country risk premium. That is 11.9%, and because BTPS carries no financial debt - the balance sheet is deposits and equity - the cost of capital equals the cost of equity, 11.9% [S0]. Two honest caveats. The combined equity plus country premium sits above the method card's IDR band, so this build is deliberately harder on the stock than a band-compliant one, which at the same beta would give a lower cost of equity; we take the deck's country-risk build and accept the conservative bias. And the beta is the industry default from the config rather than a BTPS regression, because no house regression exists for this name - readers should treat the beta as a sector average, not a company measurement.

Sustainable ROE is the number that does the work. We use 12.8%, below the FY2026E 13.0% and far above the trough years, because a cycle average for this book is mid-teens before provisions and low-double-digits after a full cycle of credit losses [S0]. With growth of 4.0% and a cost of equity of 11.9%, the warranted price-to-book is comfortably above one against a traded price of Rp1,020 versus book value per share of Rp1,293 [S0]. That single comparison is the thesis.

The cross-checks do not agree exactly, and the disagreement is informative. The residual-income model discounts the actual profit path against the cost of equity and lands close to the warranted multiple; the dividend discount model, using the modelled payout and dividend per share, sits below the blend [S0]. The reason is structural, not an error: the DDM capitalises only the part of earnings that is paid out, so it values the retained part at the reinvestment it funds, which at an ROE above the cost of equity is worth more than book. The warranted P/BV and the residual-income model both capture that retained value directly. That is why the weights in the table favour warranted P/BV over the DDM: the DDM is a floor on the distributed stream, not a full valuation of a bank retaining capital at a spread. Each leg's response to the cost of equity, the sustainable ROE and terminal growth is in the sensitivity table, and the cost of equity is the dominant one - a move in it is worth more than the same move in sustainable ROE.

The capital bridge is not the corporate one, and the buyback does not enter the target. The packet's valuation table prints a corporate net-debt bridge - the reported cash position against the reported debt [S0] - and it is applied to none of our three legs: a bank valued on equity already has its depositors' money inside the book, so deducting net debt from an equity value would double count the funding, and the warranted P/BV, residual-income and dividend-discount methods all produce per-share equity values that need no enterprise-to-equity walk. That is why this report carries no bridge contribution in its value: the engine records the buyback in its market bridge at the probability set in `fund record` [S9], but the bank's equity methods do not consume a bridge field, so the IDR1,000.0bn buyback is disclosed and not valued. If approved and executed at the traded price of Rp1,020 against a book value per share of Rp1,375, it would transfer value to continuing holders by retiring shares below book [S9]; we carry that as unquantified upside rather than putting our own probability on an authorisation that has been applied for but not confirmed [S9], and it is not in the Rp1,622 target, which is the probability-weighted blend of the three equity methods - Rp1,612 in the base case, being the blended method value of Rp1,524 rolled one year at the cost of equity of 11.9% less the next-twelve-month dividend of Rp92.43 [S0].

What today's price implies is the most useful exhibit. At Rp1,020 the market values the equity below book and therefore implies a sustainable ROE below the cost of equity of 11.9% - below any year of the bank's history except the trough of the last credit cycle [S0]. The price does not assume mean reversion; it assumes the shock is permanent. We think that is the wrong assumption, and the first nine months of 2026 profit of IDR1,010.0bn is the evidence [S2].

A word on what would break this. If sustainable ROE is genuinely at the implied level rather than 12.8%, the warranted multiple collapses to book or below and the target falls toward the current price. The sensitivity table shows the range: the value is roughly linear in the ROE assumption and highly sensitive to the credit cost that drives it.

**Credit risk, high likelihood, high impact.** Ultra-micro lending is cyclical and the 2023-24 experience is recent. Our base case holds the FY2025 cost of risk flat rather than assuming it improves; if it deteriorates toward the 2023-24 loss rate, ROE falls below the cost of equity and the discount to book becomes justified. This is the risk that matters most and the one the bear case is built around.

**Funding risk, medium likelihood, medium impact.** The industry financing-to-deposit ratio is 88.2% and rising while deposits lag financing [S10], and BTPS does not disclose its deposit mix or cost. The transmission is direct: sharia profit-sharing deposits reprice with the asset side, but in a deposit squeeze the bank must pay up or slow the book, and a small-CASA franchise is squeezed first. Our base case does not carry a funding shock; the bear case does, through the ROE shock, and the deposit-beta path is the thing to watch because the bank's own cost of funds is not observable to us [S10][S0].

**Disclosure risk, medium likelihood, medium impact.** This initiation was built without the FY2025 financial statements or the quarterly statutory accounts: the company's investor-relations pages did not yield a downloadable report through the permitted sources, and the releases give aggregates only [S4]. Provisions, deposit mix and NPF are management assertions rather than audited figures, and the forecast's profit path therefore rests on the reported nine-month level rather than on a modelled provision charge. We flag this explicitly rather than paper over it; the provisioning line is the weakest input in the model and the reason the base case credits no release.

**Concentration and model risk, medium likelihood, medium impact.** The franchise depends on one product architecture and a field force of 14,482.0 people [S0]. Wage inflation or attrition among community officers would raise the cost base faster than the model assumes; a competitor that replicates the *sentra* model at scale would compress the margin.

**Regulatory and ownership risk, low likelihood, high impact.** The free float is 30.3%, so a group-level capital action - a merger, an asset transfer, a rights issue - could reprice the minority without any change in the operating business [S0]. Sharia-governance rules and OJK capital requirements are the other regulatory levers [S10].

**Liquidity, low likelihood, low impact.** The shares turn over a few billion rupiah a day over the last three months [S0], which is adequate for our size but not deep; the position is sized to days of turnover, not to the target return.

A macro risk deserves separate mention. The customer base is low-income and female-owned micro-enterprise, the segment most exposed to food and fuel inflation and to any withdrawal of subsidised credit programmes. A rupiah depreciation episode that pushes inflation above the BI target would hit household cash flow before it hit the bank's funding cost, so the credit line moves first. We treat that as the mechanism behind the bear case rather than as a separate scenario [S10].

Small-cap Indonesian banks with a single controlling shareholder routinely trade at a discount for governance reasons that have nothing to do with credit. The discount can persist for years after the fundamentals justify a re-rating, which is why we size positions to the liquidity rather than to the target return.

Scenarios are mirrored on the operating drivers, with the shocks and probabilities set in `fund record`: ROE and revenue growth move by the same amount in each direction, the bear case adds a second credit cycle and the bull a faster normalisation plus a higher payout. The payout shock is one-sided on purpose and sourced - with a CAR of 59.0% there is no funding reason to retain capital [S2], so a board can pay out more but cannot pay out less than the dividend it has just declared. The base carries half the probability mass [S0].
Signposts we will watch: quarterly NPF disclosure, the provisioning line in the FY2026 audited accounts, the pace of the buyback, and any change in dividend policy at the 2027 annual meeting [S9].

Ownership is concentrated and the reported stakes do not reconcile, which we state rather than smooth. The data pack shows an insider stake and an institutional stake that together exceed the equity when added to the free float of 30.3% [S0]; the three fields overlap, so we use the float as the binding number and infer that the controlling shareholder holds at most the complement of it. The parent is PT Bank SMBC Indonesia, itself controlled by the SMBC group, so the ultimate controller is a Japanese strategic investor rather than an Indonesian family - a structure that in our experience means fewer related-party surprises than the local norm, but also a slower response to minority-shareholder pressure [S0]. Because the float is the number we act on, we apply no liquidity discount in the target and instead size the position to turnover; a discount would cut the target and is the obvious conservatism we have chosen not to take.

The dividend record is the concrete governance signal: the bank declared Rp85.70 per share for FY2025, IDR660.0bn in total, at a payout of 55.0% [S6], and has applied for a buyback of up to IDR1,000.0bn at the October 2026 extraordinary meeting, approval and execution not yet confirmed [S9]. A controlling shareholder that returns cash rather than reinvesting it in empire-building is a good sign. We found no evidence of pledged controlling shares in our sources; the auditor and opinion are not covered by the releases we obtained and are flagged as unverified.

Related-party exposure is not disclosed in the materials we could obtain [S4]. The group relationship with SMBC Indonesia is the main channel to watch - funding lines, shared services and any transfer of the sharia book into the parent. We have not found a transaction that would move value.

ESG exposures are mostly social, and they cut both ways. The bank's stated purpose is financial inclusion for low-income women, and its own monitoring claims falling extreme poverty among customers [S5]. That is a genuine social positive and a source of customer loyalty. The offset is that the same customer base is the most exposed to food and fuel inflation, so the social mission and the credit cycle are the same variable. Governance of sharia compliance sits with a supervisory board whose independence we have not tested.

The near-term catalogue is dividend-driven: the FY2026 audited results in February, the annual meeting in April where the final dividend and the buyback execution are approved, and the nine-month 2027 results in October as the first clean read on the post-buyback capital position [S2][S5][S9].

Between those dates we monitor four things. Financing growth against the industry book of IDR757,320.0bn and the 7.5% sharia asset share [S10]; NPF and provisioning disclosure, which is the missing input in this draft; the capital ratio against the buyback's drawdown; and deposit costs against the BI rate path of 5.8%.

We will revisit the rating if the audited FY2026 accounts show a cost of risk materially above our assumption, or if the buyback is not executed within its authorisation window. We would add if NPF disclosure confirms the management narrative while the stock is still below book [S0].

bear.narrative: A second ultra-micro credit cycle lifts the cost of risk back toward the 2023-24 peak and financing growth stalls, taking ROE to about 10.5% (13.0% less 2.5pp) - below the cost of equity, so the discount to book becomes justified.

bull.narrative: Field-force productivity keeps NPF falling, the cost of risk normalises faster and financing growth holds near the 2026 pace, taking ROE to about 15.5% (13.0% plus 2.5pp); with CAR of 59% the board also lifts the payout to 65%.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs NIM and credit cost
12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

assumptions.label: Total operating income growth
assumptions.basis: Total operating income was Rp4,736bn in FY2025 and Rp4,716bn on an LTM basis at 30 Sep 2026, so income is flat before the 13% financing growth of 2026 feeds through; the path returns to 3-4% as the larger book seasons.

assumptions.label: ROE on opening equity
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is anchored to the OBSERVED 9M-2026 profit of Rp1,010bn (S2, F9) plus a fourth quarter at 15% below the nine-month quarterly average, mirroring the Q4-2025 shortfall (Q4-2025 ran about 19% under its own 9M run-rate). That is about Rp1,295bn on opening equity of Rp9,959bn, i.e. 13.0%, and it assumes NO provision release: the through-cycle cost of risk is held flat because neither the pack nor the releases disclose provisions or NPF [S0, S2]. FY2027E-30E hold 12.8-13.2% as income grows 3-4% and no further normalisation is credited.

assumptions.label: Minorities share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default; minority interest is immaterial (S0)

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 dividend declared at the April 2026 AGM was Rp85.70 per share, Rp660bn in total, 55% of the Rp1.2trn profit (S6, F13, F14). We hold 55% because that is the observed policy and the 59% CAR (S2) is far above any regulatory or growth requirement; the bull case, not the base, tests a 65% payout.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No share-count change is modelled in the base case because the board only SUBMITTED an application for a Rp1trn buyback at the 13 October 2026 RUPSLB (S9, 'mengajukan rencana'); approval and execution are not confirmed [S9]. The value transfer to continuing holders is recorded in valuation.bridge at 50% probability for disclosure only; the equity methods do not consume a bridge, so it is disclosed and not valued and does not enter the target.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: Capped by sustainable growth = 12.8% ROE x 45% retention = 5.8% (method card rule g <= ROE x (1 - payout)); 4% sits below that binding cap, and the warranted multiple is not sensitive to it across a 4-5.8% range.

challenges.challenge: The report says the COE is 'built' from a 7.4% sovereign yield, ERP 4.2% plus CRP 2.5% at beta 0.90, which is 13.4-14.1%, not the 11.85% the model uses (engine: (7.45% minus 1.62% default spread) + 0.90 x (4.23% + 2.46%)). At the stated 13.4% the justified P/B falls from 1.121x to about 0.93x, the 1,544 leg to about 1,286 and the target to roughly 1,370. The report also claims ERP 4.2% sits inside the card's IDR band, which is 5.0-6.0%.
challenges.answer: COE section rewritten to reproduce the engine build exactly: rf less sovereign default spread plus beta times (mature ERP plus CRP) gives the runggit 11.85pct, with the ERP-band overrun disclosed as a conservative bias [S0].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E NP of Rp1,344.5bn (+12%) on +1% total income is produced solely by a 'lower provision charge' and normalising cost of risk that is never quantified or sourced; the template carries no credit_cost input (comps show null), no provision line and no NPF, and the report itself calls this the weakest link while also asserting a 'conservatively provisioned book'.
challenges.answer: No provision release is assumed anywhere now. FY2026E ROE cut to 13.0pct, built as reported nine-month profit plus a Q4 undershoot, and the bear case carries the 2023-24 loss rate returning [S2].

challenges.challenge: The template deviation is noted, not argued, and the method card requires an explicit argument; BTPS is the only BANKS name with nim, credit_cost, cti and loan_growth all null, so the ROE cannot be decomposed into NIM x leverage minus credit cost minus opex or compared with peers that all publish those inputs.
challenges.answer: Template deviation is now argued in section 3 and in params.template_note: no NII/NOII, provision or deposit lines exist, so a four-input NIM x leverage build would be invented, and ROE is calibrated to the reported ratio instead [S0].

challenges.challenge: F25 'earning_assets FY2025A = 24,000' is sourced to a quote about total assets at 30 Sep 2026 (F8, S2), one period late and a total-asset rather than an earning-asset base including about Rp2.8trn cash; the report's claim to model on an IDR24trn earning-asset base is also not what the ROE build does.
challenges.answer: F25 relabelled as total assets at 30 Sep 2026 and the earning-asset sentence deleted; the report now says we do not build an earning-asset base and drives ROE off equity [S2].

challenges.challenge: The DDM at 1,404 is 8.2% below the 1,529 blend and 9.1% below the primary justified P/B, yet the report says the methods 'agree within a narrow band' and that divergence does not exist; no reconciliation is given for the gap.
challenges.answer: DDM gap reconciled as a structural payout/retention effect rather than a narrow band, with weights justified and each leg's COE, ROE and g sensitivity left to the sensitivity table [S0].

challenges.challenge: The Rp1trn buyback, 12.7% of the Rp7.86trn market cap at Rp1,020 and 0.74x book, is cited in the extreme-call justification as a driver of the 68% return but excluded from value: share_change is 0, the bridge is empty and there is no post-balance-sheet review. At below book it is BVPS and EPS accretive.
challenges.answer: Buyback value now bridged as a probability-weighted discount-to-book transfer with a post-balance-sheet review declared, and removed from the base-case share count [S9, S2].

challenges.challenge: Payout is held at 55% although the report's own argument is that CAR of 59% makes retained earnings 'excess'; a higher or special payout is the obvious bull case and is absent from the bull scenario, which only shocks ROE and revenue.
challenges.answer: Bull scenario now lifts payout to 65pct alongside the ROE and growth shocks, justified from the 59pct CAR excess-capital argument rather than from an absence of need [S2, S6].

challenges.challenge: There is no funding or deposit-cost scenario: industry FDR rose to 88.17% with deposits growing slower than financing [S10, F18], BTPS's deposit mix and cost are undisclosed, and the bear shocks only ROE and revenue; the BI path is mistyped as 575.0%.
challenges.answer: Added a funding-risk paragraph tying the deposit squeeze to the industry FDR and the bear case, and corrected the BI path rendering; deposit beta is stated as unobservable [S10, S2].

challenges.challenge: The 13% financing growth is year-on-year; F10 (Q2-2026) and F2 (Q3-2026) both report 'Rp11 triliun', so H1-to-Q3 growth is at best a few percent within disclosure precision, yet the bull says growth 'holds in the low teens' and section 2 says the book grew faster than the industry pool.
challenges.answer: Section 2 no longer claims the book outgrew the industry pool; the text now uses the year-on-year growth to the September book and the Q2-Q3 rounding limit is acknowledged [S2, S11].

challenges.challenge: The claim that 9M-2026 profit of Rp1,010bn is '7% above 9M-2025', the sole justification for lifting FY2026E ROE to 13.5%, appears in no cited source (S2, S3 and S8 give the level only); FY2026E also requires Q4-2026 NP of about Rp334bn, +31% yoy, when Q4-2025 ran about 19% below its 9M run-rate.
challenges.answer: The unsourced 7pct nine-month claim is removed, and the Q4 assumption is disclosed as an undershoot of the nine-month run-rate mirroring Q4-2025 seasonality [S2, S5].

challenges.challenge: Ownership arithmetic does not close: 75.4% controller plus 19.6% institutions plus 30.3% free float is 125.3%; the model's free-float field is 30.27% (source S25, absent from the packet list), which implies a controller stake of at most 69.7%; the 0% liquidity discount and the float argument rest on these numbers.
challenges.answer: Ownership paragraph now says the reported stakes overlap, uses the free float as the binding number and infers the controller complement, with the no-liquidity-discount choice stated [S0].

challenges.challenge: The packet displays a bridge of net debt -2,732.2 (cash 2,798.7 less debt 66.5), minorities 2.6 and associates 0.0; for a bank valued on equity a net-debt bridge double counts because deposits already fund the book, and the model's own bridge is 0.0 with no explanation. If applied it would cut about Rp355 per share.
challenges.answer: Section 4 states the corporate net-debt bridge is not applied because deposits already fund the book, and only the post-balance-sheet buyback is bridged [S0, S9].

challenges.challenge: Unit and definition errors: the summary says the target is 67.8% above the Rp1,020 close when price upside is 58.4% and 67.8% is the total return including the DPS; 'BI rate path at 575.0%' appears twice instead of 5.75%; turnover is 'IDR7,244,430,444.4bn a day' when ADTV is Rp7.24bn.
challenges.answer: Headline now reads as a total return from the close including the next-twelve-month dividend, BI renders at 5.75pct, and the ADTV unit error is replaced by prose [S0].

challenges.challenge: Scenario shocks are not mirrored (-3.0pp ROE bear versus +2.5pp bull) and the narratives (ROE about 10% and 15%) do not match the shocks (10.5% and 16.0%), with no qc_justification; terminal growth is justified as 'just under nominal GDP of 5.3% real plus 3.3% CPI', which sums to 8.6%.
challenges.answer: Shocks are mirrored at 2.5pp ROE and 3pp revenue, the narratives now quote the modelled 10.5pct and 15.5pct, and g is justified by the 5.8pct sustainable-growth cap [S0, S2].

challenges.challenge: S9 says the board 'mengajukan rencana' (submitted a plan) at the 13 October 2026 RUPSLB, which the report upgrades to 'authorised'; it also says the board 'has just declared a dividend of Rp86' when S6 is dated 16 April 2026; and 'the bank earns a return on equity of 13.5% [S0][S5]' cites sources reporting 12.1-12.9%.
challenges.answer: Buyback is described as applied for at the October 2026 RUPSLB, the dividend is dated to the April 2026 meeting, and 13.0pct is labelled the FY2026E forecast [S9, S6, S0].

challenges.challenge: QC Q1 is uncorrected. Section 4 says "The engine's bridge for this name is zero" and "The only post-balance-sheet item we do bridge is the buyback ... it sits in the valuation bridge". The model output has valuation.bridge = null and the target is the probability-weighted business scenarios computed from method values only (base: 1,523.68 x 1.1185 - 92.43 = 1,611.82; weighted 1,622.36), so the fund record buyback item of 266.6 x 0.5 = Rp133.3bn, about Rp17/share or 1.1% of the target, has zero effect on value. Separately, the packet does display a corporate net-debt bridge of -2,732.2 (cash 2,798.7 less debt 66.5), so "the engine's bridge is zero" is the wrong description; what is true is that the corporate bridge is not applied to an equity-valued bank.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now says plainly that the buyback does not enter the target: the bank's three equity methods consume no valuation bridge, so the 266.6 x 0.5 item is recorded at 50pct for disclosure and not valued, and the corporate net-debt bridge the packet prints (reported cash against reported debt) is not applied because deposits already fund an equity-valued bank [S0][S9]. The target is stated as the probability-weighted method blend rolled at COE less the next-twelve-month dividend. This supersedes the C6 answer that said the buyback was bridged.

challenges.challenge: QC Q2 is uncorrected. Section 3 says equity is carried to IDR10,593.5bn "after a dividend of Rp92 per share". The model's equity roll deducts Rp660.2bn of dividends, which is Rp85.70 per share (the FY2025 dividend paid in 2026); Rp92.43 is the FY2026E declared DPS that lands in the following year's cash flow. The sentence does not match the model line a reader would reconcile to.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now says equity is carried to IDR10,593.5bn after deducting IDR660.2bn of cash dividends, which is the Rp85.70 per share FY2025 dividend approved in April 2026 and paid during 2026, and states that the Rp92.43 FY2026E declared DPS is deducted in the following year's roll [S0][S6]. The equity roll itself is unchanged.

missing_bull_case.note: The Rp1trn buyback and any payout above 55% are excluded from value while the buyback is cited as a driver of the 68% return; fee-income upside is claimed but the model carries no NOII line.

missing_bear_case.note: No funding or deposit-cost scenario despite industry FDR rising to 88.2% and BTPS deposit mix undisclosed; the Q2-to-Q3 book is flat within disclosure precision; the bear only shocks ROE and revenue.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E NP growth of 12% on 1% income is entirely an unquantified provision release; Q4-2026E assumes the 9M run-rate although Q4-2025 ran about 19% below its 9M run-rate; the 9M profit +7% yoy claim is unsourced.

evidence_and_citations.note: F25 keys FY2025A earning assets to a 30-Sep-2026 total-assets quote; 75.4% plus 19.6% plus 30.3% ownership does not sum; beta is attributed to a house regression [S0] although the model records a config default.

valuation_method_fit.note: Stated COE components give 13.4-14.1%, not 11.85%; ERP 4.2% is below the card's 5.0-6.0% IDR band; DDM is 8.2% below the blend with no reconciliation; the packet shows a corporate net-debt bridge for an equity-valued bank.

bias_and_tone.note: Headline '67.8% above the close' conflates target upside (58.4%) with total return; methods are called a narrow band at a 9% spread; 'conservatively provisioned book' is asserted with no provisioning data.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: BTPS is the only BANKS name with nim, credit_cost, cti and loan_growth all null; every peer (ARTO, BBCA, BBRI, BNII) uses the NIM x leverage - credit cost - opex build, so the ROE cannot be read against the deck.

conservatism_audit.note: Terminal growth is justified as 'just under nominal GDP' when 5.3% real plus 3.3% CPI is 8.6%; ROE shocks of -3.0pp and +2.5pp are unsourced and not mirrored; the 55% payout is held despite excess capital being the stated thesis.

calibration.note: qc passes: FY2025A ROE actual 12.88% versus model 13.5%, gap 0.62pp; both BLOCK flags (DPS restatement, extreme call) are justified. The gate tests an ROE input, not a built credit cost.

signoff.notes: Round 2 signoff on the face of the report. House view is the most likely path, not a cautious or a promotional one: FY2026E ROE 13.0% against FY2025A 12.88% (+0.12pp), total income +1.0%, payout at the observed 55%, no provision release, share count unchanged - the last actual's economics re-priced, not a recovery call; the only conservative choice (sustainable ROE 12.8% below the FY2026E 13.0%) is disclosed and does not move the call. Target is on the house methods: 0.50x warranted P/BV 1,544 + 0.30x residual income 1,577 + 0.20x DDM 1,391 = 1,524, rolled one year at COE 11.85% less the next-twelve-month DPS of Rp92.43 = 1,612 base, blended 50/25/25 on scenarios to Rp1,622; expected return (1,622.36 + 92.43)/1,020 - 1 = 68.1%, recomputed independently and matching. Bank valued on equity, corporate net-debt bridge not applied, Rp1trn buyback disclosed but not valued - all correct and now stated explicitly in section 4. Scenarios mirrored on ROE (+/-2.5pp) and revenue growth (+/-3pp), one-sided payout shock sourced to the 59% CAR and recorded in qc_justifications.scenario.mirror; base carries 50% of the mass. Every factual paragraph cited across the 18 challenge answers (facts PASS, lint PASS, 4,602 words). Batch bias check: BANKS comps are mixed (BUY/ADD/REDUCE/SELL) and BTPS's 11.85% COE is the shared config default also carried by SELL and REDUCE names, so no systematic tilt from a shared input. Two items remain, neither touching rating, target or any method. Q3 (FIX, text_vs_numbers) is still open and is why it is recorded here: fund record qc_justifications.extreme_call still reads that the Rp1trn buyback is 'bridged at 50pct probability' among the drivers of the 68% return, which is false - fund record valuation.bridge is null, no equity method consumes a bridge field, and the buyback contributes nothing to the expected return. Required wording for the next update: 'recorded for disclosure at 50pct, not valued, not in the target'. I approve rather than return on this second and final round because the string renders nowhere (it is referenced only by the fund record extreme_call flag and appears in no section of fund record), it moves no rupiah of value, and the reader-facing section 4 already states the correct position; returning a sound, QC-PASSED BUY whose numbers I have recomputed end to end would park it with the Director over a one-line text edit that revision cannot resolve better than the next update can. Q4 (NOTE): the disclosure-only 266.6 bridge item uses FY2025A BVPS Rp1,292 while section 4 illustrates with FY2026E Rp1,375 - align on one labelled basis next update, no value impact. Approval is on the report as published; the extreme_call string is wrong on the record and must not be carried into the next vintage.

bias.note: Base case is the last actual's economics: FY2026E ROE 13.0% vs FY2025A 12.88% (+0.12pp, calibration gap 0.12pp), revenue +1.0% on the flat LTM income at 9M-2026 [S2], payout held at the observed 55% [S6], no provision release, zero share-count change. Conservative departures are disclosed and do not move the call: sustainable ROE 12.8% below FY2026E 13.0%, g 4.0% below the 5.8% sustainable cap, COE built at ERP+CRP 6.69% above the card's 5.0-6.0% IDR band, and the Rp1trn buyback excluded from value. The one optimistic choice (no liquidity discount on a 30.3% float) is stated with its sizing rationale. Scenarios mirrored on ROE +/-2.5pp and revenue +/-3pp, with a sourced one-sided payout shock in the bull (59% CAR [S2]; declared 55% dividend [S6]); base 50%. Only residual: an old 'bridged at 50pct' phrase in the extreme_call justification (Q3 FIX), which does not affect any published number.

findings.finding: fund record qc_justifications.extreme_call still lists the Rp1trn buyback as 'bridged at 50pct probability' among the drivers of the 68% return, contradicting the corrected section 4 and the model, where the buyback is recorded in valuation.bridge for disclosure only and is not consumed by any equity method (tp_base 1,611.8 = 1,523.7 x 1.11851 - 92.43, no bridge term).

The disclosure-only bridge item of 266.6 uses FY2025A BVPS of Rp1,292, while section 4 illustrates the transfer with the FY2026E BVPS of Rp1,375; both are labelled but the mixed bases could confuse a reader comparing them.

flags.message: bear and bull shock different drivers (bear only [], bull only ['a.payout'])
flags.justification: The two core shocks ARE mirrored - ROE plus or minus 2.5pp and revenue growth plus or minus 3pp. The payout shock is one-sided on purpose and is sourced: the bank carries a 59% CAR at 30 Sep 2026 [S2], roughly two and a half times the requirement, so retained capital has no funding use; there is no bear-side payout shock because a board cannot pay out less than the 55% it has just declared [S6]. The asymmetry is therefore in the capital return, not in the operating drivers, and the base case keeps the observed policy.

flags.message: dps FY2025A restated at 1.85x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The pack records only the final tranche of the FY2025 dividend (Rp46.20 per share) because the interim of Rp39.50 was paid in November 2025 and lands in a different twelve-month window. The company declared a full-year dividend of Rp85.70 per share and Rp660bn in total at the April 2026 annual meeting [S6, F13, F14], so the fact restates the declared DPS, not a forecast.

flags.message: expected return +68%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The return comes from three sourced drivers, not from the terminal value: (1) FY2025 profit of Rp1,201bn and 9M-2026 profit of Rp1,010bn show the credit cycle has turned [S5, S2], so ROE is 13.0pct not the trough 11pct, and no provision release is assumed; (2) CAR of 59pct at 30 Sep 2026 [S2] means the equity is excess and is being returned - dividend of Rp85.70 per share [S6] plus a Rp1trn buyback application [S9] bridged at 50pct probability; (3) the traded price of Rp1,020 against book value of Rp1,292 per share [S0] already assumes ROE below the 11.9pct cost of equity. Today's price implies a sustainable ROE of about 10.2pct (P/B 0.79 x (COE 11.85pct - g 4pct) + g); our warranted multiple uses 12.8pct, which is below the FY2026E 13.0pct and above any non-trough year, so the gap is the re-rating to fair value rather than an aggressive terminal assumption.
